sections.html: Geophagus brasiliensis is one of the very first cichlids to become available in the aquarium hobby. It was first imported to Germany around 1900. It is capable of reproduction at 6–8 cm but can grow to over 20 cm under favorable conditions. They are open-brooding cichlids, and both parents care for their young.

The name Geophagus brasiliensis encompasses several species that are very similar to one another. None of them actually belong to the genus Geophagus in the strict sense, which comprises the earth-eaters related to G. altifrons. For this reason, the genus name is often written in quotation marks when referring to the brasiliensis group. A comprehensive revision does not yet exist.

It is important never to breed Geophagus from the brasiliensis group that originate from different locations. For example, the "variant" G. iporangensis, now generally recognized as a distinct species, was described in 1911 from São Paulo. Hybrids are undesirable in the hobby.

The species is native to the southern part of South America. The wild-caught specimens currently available come from Brazil, specifically the state of São Paulo, and were collected in the area around the city of Botucatu. Hydrologically, the area belongs to the Rio Tietê watershed.
Larger cichlids should be housed in larger aquariums. The smaller the aquarium, the more problematic it is to keep them with other fish.

G. brasiliensis is completely undemanding regarding water parameters. In the wild, they are even occasionally found in brackish water. The species tolerates low water temperatures. Room temperature is sufficient for maintenance; for breeding, you can raise the temperature to 24–26°C.

Geophagus brasiliensis are avid burrowers; this should be taken into account when setting up the tank. Plants are best placed in pots, or you can forgo plants that root in the substrate altogether. Floating plants are a good alternative.

They will eat any ornamental fish food of a suitable size, though it should be quite substantial and nutritious. It has even been observed that these fish eat Malaysian trumpet snails (Melanoides), which are otherwise spurned by nearly all snail-eating fish.
Robust and fast-swimming fish species make suitable tank mates.
They are open-brooding cichlids, and both parents care together for their young. Reproduction is possible at 6–8 cm; for breeding, the temperature can be raised to 24–26°C.
